A mileage deduction calculator is a tool that multiplies the miles you drove for a deductible purpose by the IRS standard mileage rate to estimate your write-off. For tax year 2025 the rates are 70 cents per business mile, 21 cents per medical or moving mile (moving applies only to active-duty Armed Forces), and 14 cents per charitable mile, which is fixed by statute. The standard-mileage method is an alternative to deducting your actual vehicle costs, so you pick one or the other. Enter your miles by category and the tool returns each deduction and the total. It’s an estimate, not tax advice. Try it now Open Mileage Deduction Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗

Freelancers, gig drivers, and small-business owners rack up deductible business miles all year. Entering your total business miles at the 2025 rate of 70 cents each turns a mileage-log number into an estimated deduction in seconds, so you can gauge the tax value of that driving before you file and plan quarterly estimated payments more accurately.

Miles driven in service of a qualified charity are deductible at 14 cents each if you itemize, and many volunteers never claim them. Adding up trips to deliver meals, transport supplies, or drive for an organization and multiplying by the charitable rate shows a deduction that would otherwise go unused — provided you keep a record of the trips.
documents.s: Value charitable driving you might overlook

documents.t: Miles driven for medical care may be deductible at 21 cents if you itemize and clear the medical-expense threshold, and the same rate covers moving miles — but only for active-duty military moving under orders. The calculator keeps these two 21-cent uses separate from business and charitable driving so you apply the right rate to the right miles.
documents.s: Check medical or Armed Forces moving miles

documents.t: The standard-mileage method is one of two ways to deduct vehicle costs; the other totals your actual gas, maintenance, insurance, and depreciation. This tool computes the standard-mileage figure so you have a clean number to weigh against your actual costs. Drivers with an efficient, paid-off car often come out ahead on standard mileage, while expensive vehicles may favor actual expenses.
documents.s: Compare standard mileage to actual expenses

documents.t: Seeing your mileage deduction grow as the year goes on encourages consistent logging and can inform late-year decisions, like whether to bundle deductible errands. Because the deduction is only as good as your records, using the calculator alongside a contemporaneous mileage log — date, purpose, and miles for each trip — keeps your estimate defensible if the IRS ever asks.

Gather your mileage by purpose — From your log, total the miles you drove for each deductible category: business, medical, moving, and charitable. Enter business miles — Type your business miles; the tool multiplies them by the 2025 rate of 70 cents to estimate that deduction. Enter medical or moving miles — Add medical miles, or moving miles if you are active-duty military; both use the 21-cent rate. Enter charitable miles — Add miles driven for a qualified charity, which the tool multiplies by the statutory 14-cent rate. Read your per-category and total deduction — Each category shows its own dollar figure and they are summed into an estimated total mileage deduction for 2025.

Input: 12,000 business miles Output: $8,400 estimated business deduction Input: 500 charitable miles Output: $70 estimated charitable deduction Input: 800 medical miles Output: $168 estimated medical deduction

What are the 2025 IRS standard mileage rates? For 2025 they are 70 cents per business mile, 21 cents per medical or moving mile, and 14 cents per charitable mile. The charitable rate is set by statute and does not change with inflation like the others. Who can deduct business miles? Self-employed people and business owners can deduct business driving. Since 2018, most W-2 employees cannot deduct unreimbursed business mileage, so this generally applies to independent workers rather than employees. Can anyone claim the moving-mile rate? No. Since the 2017 tax law, the moving-expense deduction — including the 21-cent moving-mile rate — is available only to active-duty members of the Armed Forces moving under military orders. Standard mileage or actual expenses — which should I use? It depends on your vehicle and costs. Standard mileage is simpler and often better for fuel-efficient or paid-off cars; actual expenses can win for costly vehicles. There are rules about switching methods, so check IRS guidance. Do I need a mileage log? Yes. The IRS expects a contemporaneous record showing the date, destination, purpose, and miles of each trip. Without one, a deduction can be disallowed if you are audited. This tool does the math but does not keep your log. Does this compute depreciation or actual costs? No. It only applies the standard mileage rates. It does not calculate the actual-expense method, vehicle depreciation, lease costs, or the depreciation component built into the business rate. Is this tax advice, and is my data stored? It is an educational estimate, not tax advice, and everything runs in your browser with nothing uploaded. Confirm eligibility and amounts with the IRS or a tax professional.

Keep a contemporaneous log — date, purpose, and miles per trip — so your deduction holds up under audit. Don’t mix categories; business, medical, moving, and charitable miles each use a different rate. Commuting from home to your regular workplace is not deductible business mileage. Only active-duty military moving under orders can use the 21-cent moving-mile rate. Compare this standard-mileage estimate with your actual vehicle costs before deciding which method to claim.

A net worth calculator is a tool that subtracts everything you owe from everything you own to produce a single figure — your net worth — that captures your overall financial position at one moment. You total your assets (cash, bank balances, investments, retirement accounts, real estate, vehicles, and other property, each at current market value) and your liabilities (mortgage, student and auto loans, credit-card balances, and any other debt, each at its payoff amount), and the difference is the result. It can be negative early in life, which is completely normal. The tool also derives a debt-to-asset ratio, where lower is stronger. Everything runs in your browser; nothing is uploaded. This is an estimate, not financial advice. Try it now Open Net Worth Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗

Income tells you what flows in, but net worth tells you what you actually keep. A high earner who spends everything can have a lower net worth than a modest earner who saves and invests steadily. Recalculating every month or quarter turns an abstract goal into a number you can watch climb, and it rewards paying down debt just as much as growing savings.
documents.s: Measure real progress instead of income

documents.t: Two people can share the same net worth while one is far more exposed, because a large asset pile propped up by heavy borrowing is fragile. The debt-to-asset ratio shows what fraction of what you own is still owed. Tracking it alongside the headline figure highlights whether your position is genuinely strengthening or simply riding rising asset prices.
documents.s: Watch the debt-to-asset ratio, not just the total

documents.t: Before taking on a mortgage, buying a car, or paying off a loan early, you can enter the before-and-after numbers and see how each choice moves your net worth and debt-to-asset ratio. That makes the trade-off concrete — a new car may add an asset but a larger loan, while an early payoff shrinks both sides — so you can weigh decisions with real figures rather than a hunch.
documents.s: See the effect of a big financial decision

documents.t: Listing assets and liabilities in categories creates a simple personal balance sheet you can reproduce on a schedule. Keeping the same categories each time makes snapshots comparable, so you can spot which parts of your finances are growing and which are stalling. It is the same idea a business uses to track its position, scaled down to a single household.
documents.s: Build a repeatable personal balance sheet

documents.t: Lenders, mortgage brokers, and financial planners often ask for a net-worth summary. Having your assets, liabilities, the total, and the debt-to-asset ratio ready in advance saves time and helps you answer their questions accurately. The figure here is a self-reported estimate rather than a verified financial statement, but it is a solid, organized starting point for that conversation.
documents.s: Prepare for a loan or planning conversation

documents.t: List your assets at market value — Enter cash, bank balances, investments, retirement accounts, real estate, vehicles, and other property using what each would sell for today, not what you paid. List your liabilities at payoff — Add your mortgage, loans, credit-card balances, and any other debt using the current amount needed to clear each one in full. Let the tool total each side — As you type, the calculator sums total assets and total liabilities so you can see both columns at a glance. Read your net worth — It subtracts total liabilities from total assets and displays the result, which may be a positive or a negative number. Check the debt-to-asset ratio — The tool divides total liabilities by total assets to show how leveraged you are; a lower ratio means a stronger, less debt-dependent position.

Input: Assets $150,000; liabilities $90,000 Output: Net worth $60,000 — debt-to-asset 0.60 Input: Assets $25,000; liabilities $40,000 Output: Net worth −$15,000 Input: Assets $500,000; liabilities $120,000 Output: Net worth $380,000 — debt-to-asset 0.24

What counts as an asset? Anything you own that has monetary value: cash and bank balances, brokerage and retirement investments, real estate, vehicles, and valuable personal property. Enter each at its current market value — what it would realistically sell for now — not its original purchase price. What counts as a liability? Any money you owe: mortgage, home-equity, student, auto, and personal loans, outstanding credit-card balances, and unpaid taxes or bills. Use the current payoff balance for each, not the original loan amount. Is a negative net worth bad? Not necessarily. Many people, especially early in a career or just after buying a home, owe more than they own because of student loans or a fresh mortgage. What matters most is whether the number trends upward over time as you pay down debt and build assets. What is a good debt-to-asset ratio? There is no single right answer; it depends on your age, goals, and the type of debt. As a general idea, a lower ratio means less of what you own is financed by borrowing, which is more resilient. Compare your own ratio over time rather than to a fixed target. How often should I calculate it? Monthly or quarterly is plenty for most people. Net worth moves slowly, and checking too often can make normal market swings feel dramatic. Using the same categories each time keeps your snapshots comparable. Is my financial data stored or uploaded? No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser. Nothing you enter is sent to a server or saved anywhere by the tool. Is this financial advice? No. It is an estimate to help you organize and track your finances. For decisions about debt, investing, or planning, consult a qualified financial professional who can consider your full situation.

Use current market values for assets and current payoff balances for debts — mixing old and new figures skews the result. Keep the same categories every time so snapshots stay comparable month to month. Update home and vehicle values periodically; they drift and can quietly change your net worth. Do not double-count — a paycheck you have already spent is not an asset, and a listed loan should appear only once. Watch the trend line over months, not a single snapshot — direction matters more than any one figure.

An operating expense calculator is a tool that computes the operating expense ratio (OER) — operating expenses divided by revenue — to show the share of every revenue dollar consumed running the business, excluding the cost of goods sold, interest, and taxes. From the same inputs it also derives gross profit, operating income, and operating margin, so you can see how much is left after both production and overhead. A lower OER is generally more efficient, but a "good" ratio varies by industry, so the number is most useful compared with peers or your own past periods. Everything is calculated in your browser, and the output is an estimate for analysis, not financial advice. Try it now Open Operating Expense Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗

The operating expense ratio tells you how much of each revenue dollar is spent keeping the business running — rent, salaries, utilities, and administration — before interest and tax. Entering revenue and operating expenses returns that share instantly, so you can see whether overhead is lean or heavy. A rising OER over time is an early warning that costs are outpacing sales, worth investigating line by line.
documents.s: Measure overhead efficiency at a glance

documents.t: Beyond the ratio, the tool derives gross profit, operating income, and operating margin from the same inputs. That lets you separate two very different problems: a thin gross profit points to pricing or cost of goods, while a healthy gross profit eaten up by overhead points to operating expenses. Seeing all three figures at once makes it clearer where profit is being made or lost.
documents.s: See gross profit and operating margin together

documents.t: Overhead tends to drift upward quietly as a business adds staff, software, and space. Calculating the OER each month or quarter surfaces that creep before it erodes margin. A ratio that climbs while revenue is flat is a signal to review recurring costs, renegotiate contracts, or pause discretionary spending — long before the annual accounts make the trend obvious.
documents.s: Compare periods to catch cost creep

documents.t: A "good" operating expense ratio depends heavily on the sector — a software company and a grocery store have very different cost structures. The calculator gives your figure so you can line it up against peers or industry averages rather than an arbitrary target. Judged in context, the ratio shows whether your overhead is competitive or leaves less room for profit than rivals.

Knowing what share of revenue overhead consumes helps you set prices that actually leave a margin and build budgets grounded in real ratios. If overhead already takes a large slice, a small price cut or cost increase can wipe out operating income. The tool makes that sensitivity visible, so pricing and spending decisions rest on the numbers rather than a hunch.

Enter total revenue — Provide net sales or revenue for the period you are analysing. Enter cost of goods sold — Add COGS so the tool can separate gross profit from operating overhead; if you have no COGS, enter zero. Enter operating expenses — Include running costs such as rent, salaries, utilities, and admin — but not interest or taxes, which sit below operating income. Read the operating expense ratio — The calculator divides operating expenses by revenue to show the share of each revenue dollar spent on overhead. Review the derived figures — It also shows gross profit, operating income, and operating margin so you can see profitability from top to bottom.

Input: Revenue $500,000; COGS $200,000; operating expenses $150,000 Output: OER 30%; gross profit $300,000; operating income $150,000; margin 30% Input: Revenue $500,000; COGS $200,000; operating expenses $250,000 Output: OER 50%; gross profit $300,000; operating income $50,000; margin 10% Input: Revenue $1,000,000; COGS $0; operating expenses $400,000 Output: OER 40%; gross profit $1,000,000; operating income $600,000; margin 60%

What is the operating expense ratio? The OER is operating expenses divided by revenue, expressed as a percentage. It shows how much of each revenue dollar is consumed running the business, excluding the cost of goods sold, interest, and taxes. What counts as an operating expense? Day-to-day running costs: rent, salaries and wages, utilities, marketing, insurance, and administration. It excludes the direct cost of goods sold, financing interest, and income taxes, which are accounted for elsewhere. Why are interest and taxes excluded? The OER measures operational efficiency, so it stops at operating income. Interest depends on how the business is financed and taxes on jurisdiction and profit — both sit below the operating line and would blur the operational picture. What is a good operating expense ratio? There is no universal figure; it varies widely by industry and business model. A lower OER generally signals more efficient overhead, but compare yours with sector peers and your own past periods rather than a single target. What is the difference between OER and operating margin? They are related views. OER is operating expenses as a share of revenue; operating margin is operating income as a share of revenue. Roughly, once COGS and opex are covered, what remains of revenue is the operating margin. Do I need cost of goods sold to use it? No. If your business has no COGS — many service firms do not — enter zero, and gross profit will equal revenue. The OER itself is based on operating expenses and revenue. Is anything I enter stored or uploaded? No. All calculations happen in your browser, and nothing you type is sent to a server or saved.

Keep cost of goods sold out of operating expenses — mixing them distorts both the OER and gross profit. Exclude interest and taxes; the OER stops at operating income by design. Compare your ratio with industry peers, since a "good" OER is sector-specific. Track the OER across periods to catch overhead creeping up faster than revenue. Use consistent period lengths for revenue and expenses so the ratio is comparable.

A palladium rate calculator computes the metal value of palladium items — used in jewelry (especially white-gold alloys), industrial applications (catalytic converters dominate global demand), and investment bars — by combining weight, purity, and spot price. The ZTools Palladium Rate Calculator runs entirely in the browser, supports the common purity standards (.950 jewelry, .500 alloyed, .9995 investment bars), gram / ounce / kilogram inputs, and is useful for jewelry valuation, catalytic-converter scrap negotiation, and investment-bar verification. Try it now Open Palladium Rate Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗
Modern petrol catalytic converters contain palladium. Recyclers price by extractable metal weight; the calculator estimates the floor value.
Some white-gold alternatives are .950 palladium. Calculate melt to gauge offers.
Confirm the spot-implied price of a 1 oz palladium bar before completing a deal.
Palladium often moves independently of gold and silver — knowing per-gram values helps right-size positions.

Enter spot palladium price — Per gram or per troy ounce. Palladium has been highly volatile in the past decade; confirm rate before transacting. Pick weight unit — Grams, ounces, kilograms. Enter purity — .950 (jewelry), .500 (alloy), .9995 (investment). Compute melt value — weight × purity × spot. Cross-check against gold/platinum — Optional comparison view; palladium trades differently from both.

Input: 6 g of .950 palladium at $30/g spot Output: 6 × 0.95 × $30 = $171 melt value Input: 1 oz palladium bar at $1,000/oz spot Output: ~$999 melt + small bar premium Input: Catalytic converter substrate, 10 g recoverable Pd at $30/g Output: ~$300 metal value before recycler margin (typically receive 60–80%)

Why is palladium so volatile? The market is small and dominated by Russian / South African supply. Auto-industry demand (gasoline catalytic converters) creates large swings when policy or production changes. Can palladium be substituted for platinum? In some catalysts and jewelry alloys, yes. The substitution flow has driven big price moves over the past decade. How does palladium jewelry compare to platinum? Cheaper per gram, lighter (less dense at 12.0 g/cc vs platinum 21.45 g/cc), similarly hypoallergenic. Are palladium bars liquid? Less liquid than gold or silver bars. Reputable refiner brands (PAMP, Credit Suisse, Royal Canadian Mint) trade more actively. Should I cash in a catalytic converter from an old car? It is often worth $50–500 depending on the vehicle and metal content. Theft of catalytic converters is a real problem because of this; sell legally with vehicle title proof. Is rhodium also in my converter? Yes — modern converters contain platinum + palladium + rhodium. Rhodium has been worth more per gram than the others at times. Recyclers price the bundle.

Confirm rate at the moment of transaction — palladium can swing 5%+ in a day. For converter scrap, get multiple quotes — recycler margins vary widely. Investment bars from recognised refiners hold value best; off-brand bars trade at larger discounts. Palladium jewelry resale market is thin — expect deep discounts to spot when selling. Diversification rule of thumb: hold no more in any one PGM (platinum group metal) than you can lose without panic.

A paycheck calculator estimates take-home pay (net pay) from gross wages by subtracting federal / state income tax, payroll taxes (Social Security + Medicare in the US, National Insurance in the UK, comparable in other countries), and pre-tax deductions (401(k), health-insurance premium, HSA / FSA contributions). The ZTools Paycheck Calculator runs in the browser, supports both salaried and hourly inputs, lets you toggle pay frequency (weekly, biweekly, semi-monthly, monthly), and is an educational estimator only — actual pay depends on local tax rules, filing status, dependants, and many edge cases; verify any number with your employer's payroll provider before making financial decisions. Try it now Open Paycheck Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗
A $90K offer in California vs $85K in Texas — federal tax is similar, but California state tax + cost-of-living shifts the real take-home meaningfully.
A consultant invoices $5K/month — what lands in the bank after self-employment tax and quarterly estimates? Calculator approximates.
Increasing 401(k) from 5% to 10% — what is the actual take-home reduction? Often less than expected due to tax savings.
$25/hour at 40 hours/week — net annual after taxes? Calculator shows both before and after deductions.

Pick pay type and frequency — Salaried (annual amount) or hourly (rate + hours). Pay frequency: weekly, biweekly, semi-monthly, monthly. Enter gross pay per period — For salaried, the calculator divides annual into per-period. Enter pre-tax deductions — 401(k) %, health-insurance premium, HSA/FSA, commuter benefits — anything pre-tax. Apply taxes — Federal tax via brackets, state tax via flat % or local schedule, FICA / NI / equivalent payroll tax. Show net pay — Gross − pre-tax deductions − taxes = take-home. Annualised view also shown.

Input: Salary $80,000, US, single, 5% 401(k), no state tax Output: Gross/biweekly $3,077 · 401(k) $154 · Federal $290 · FICA $223 · Net ~$2,410 Input: Hourly $25 × 40 hr/week, US single, 0% 401(k) Output: Gross/biweekly $2,000 · Net ~$1,580 Input: UK £50,000 salaried, default personal allowance Output: Gross/month £4,167 · Income tax £616 · NI £375 · Net ~£3,176

Why is my actual paycheck different from the calculator? Many reasons: pre-tax deductions you did not enter (insurance, HSA), additional withholdings (e.g., supplemental income), state-specific items, post-tax deductions (Roth 401(k)), bonuses. Treat as a ballpark. How is FICA calculated? US Social Security: 6.2% on wages up to the annual wage base. Medicare: 1.45% on all wages, plus 0.9% additional Medicare tax above thresholds. Total: 7.65% for most workers, employer matches. Does pre-tax deduction reduce my take-home dollar-for-dollar? No — it reduces taxable income too. So $100 pre-tax 401(k) reduces take-home by ~$70–80 depending on bracket. Effective "cost" of saving is less than the amount saved. Should I use Roth or traditional 401(k)? Depends on your tax bracket now vs in retirement. The calculator can model traditional (pre-tax) easily; Roth (post-tax) reduces take-home but produces tax-free retirement withdrawals. Are bonuses taxed differently? In the US, supplemental wages are withheld at flat 22% for the first $1M. Actual tax owed at year-end matches your normal bracket — overwithholding is refunded. Will it tell me if my employer is withholding correctly? It is an estimate. For real verification, check your year-end pay stubs vs filed taxes; significant mismatches warrant a payroll inquiry.

Treat the result as a ballpark — actual paycheck has many fine-grained inputs. For job-offer comparisons, use the same calculator for both offers — apples to apples. Pre-tax retirement savings cost less than they save — the tax break makes contributions more affordable than they look. Verify state / local tax rates for your specific jurisdiction. After a major tax-law change, recompute — withholding tables shift annually.

A payroll tax calculator is a tool that breaks down the federal FICA payroll taxes on wages for the 2025 tax year into the employee share and the matching employer share. FICA has two components. Social Security is 6.2% from each side on wages up to the 2025 wage base of $176,100, so earnings above that are not subject to it. Medicare is 1.45% from each side on all wages with no cap, plus a 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax paid by the employee alone on earnings over a filing-status threshold. This calculator shows each side and the combined cost. It is a 2025 estimate, not tax advice. Try it now Open Payroll Tax Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗

A paystub shows your FICA deduction but hides the matching amount your employer pays on your behalf. This tool lays out both sides — Social Security 6.2% each and Medicare 1.45% each — so you can see the full cost of employing you. That combined figure is useful when comparing a salaried role with contract work, where you would owe both sides yourself.
documents.s: See what you and your employer each pay

documents.t: Social Security tax stops once your year-to-date wages reach $176,100 in 2025. Entering your YTD wages lets the calculator apply the cap accurately, so a high earner mid-year sees Social Security tax taper off on the portion above the base, while Medicare, which has no cap, keeps applying to every dollar earned.
documents.s: Apply the Social Security wage base correctly mid-year

documents.t: Small-business owners and freelancers hiring help need to budget the employer share of FICA on top of gross pay. Feeding in an employee’s wage shows the 6.2% Social Security and 1.45% Medicare the employer owes, giving a clearer true cost of a hire before adding unemployment tax, benefits, and other overhead the tool does not cover.
documents.s: Estimate an employer’s payroll cost per employee

documents.t: Self-employed people do not split FICA with an employer; they pay both halves as self-employment tax — 12.4% Social Security up to the wage base and 2.9% Medicare. Comparing the two-sided employee breakdown here with that single self-employed total makes the difference concrete when weighing a W-2 job against 1099 work.

FICA on a paystub should equal 6.2% and 1.45% of that period’s wages, and the 0.9% Additional Medicare should appear only after year-to-date wages pass $200,000. Entering the same figures here lets you confirm the numbers line up, so a payroll error — a missed wage-base cap, a wrong rate, or the surtax applied too early — is easy to spot before it compounds across the year.

Enter the gross wages — Type the wage amount you want to analyse for 2025; the rates apply to this figure. Add year-to-date wages — Provide wages already earned this year so the tool knows how much of the $176,100 Social Security base remains. Select the filing status — This sets the threshold for the employee-only 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on high earnings. Review the employee side — See the employee’s 6.2% Social Security (subject to the cap), 1.45% Medicare, and any 0.9% surtax. Review the employer side and totals — See the employer’s matching 6.2% and 1.45% (no 0.9% match), plus the combined payroll-tax total.

Input: $5,000 wage, $0 YTD, single Output: Employee $382.50, Employer $382.50 Input: $10,000 wage, $175,000 YTD, single Output: Social Security taxed on only $1,100 Input: $20,000 wage, $250,000 YTD, single Output: No Social Security; 0.9% surtax applies

What taxes count as payroll (FICA) tax? FICA is the combination of Social Security tax (6.2% each from employee and employer) and Medicare tax (1.45% each), plus the employee-only 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax on high earnings. It does not include federal or state income tax withholding. What is the 2025 Social Security wage base? It is $176,100. Social Security tax of 6.2% applies only to wages up to that amount each year; earnings above it are not subject to Social Security tax, though Medicare tax continues with no cap. Does the employer pay the 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax too? No. The 0.9% surtax is paid by the employee only and is never matched by the employer. The employer matches the 6.2% Social Security and 1.45% Medicare, but not the additional 0.9%. Why do you ask for year-to-date wages? Because the Social Security cap and the 0.9% surtax threshold are annual. Knowing wages already earned this year lets the tool apply the $176,100 cap and the $200,000 withholding point correctly for a mid-year paycheck. Does this include income tax or take-home pay? No. It calculates FICA payroll tax only, not federal or state income tax. For net pay after all taxes and deductions, use a dedicated paycheck calculator. How is it different for the self-employed? The self-employed pay both the employee and employer halves themselves through self-employment tax — 12.4% Social Security up to the wage base and 2.9% Medicare — rather than splitting it with an employer. Is my wage information stored? No. All calculations run in your browser, and nothing you enter is uploaded or saved.

Use Medicare or Social Security wages from your paystub, which can differ from taxable income because pre-tax retirement contributions still count for FICA. Keep year-to-date wages current so the Social Security cap applies at the right point in the year. Remember the employer’s 6.2% + 1.45% is a real cost of hiring, useful when pricing contract work. For total take-home, pair this with the Paycheck Calculator, which adds income tax withholding. Treat the numbers as a 2025 estimate and confirm specifics with a payroll professional or the IRS.

A platinum rate calculator computes the metal value of platinum jewelry, coins, or bars by combining weight, purity (most jewelry-grade platinum is .950 — 95% pure — though .900 and .850 are used in some markets), and the current platinum spot price. The ZTools Platinum Rate Calculator runs entirely in the browser, supports gram / ounce / kilogram inputs, all common purity stamps, and includes notes on why platinum and gold prices have decoupled in recent years (industrial demand for catalytic converters, supply concentration in South Africa, less consumer-jewelry demand than gold) — context that affects whether melt value is the right benchmark. Try it now Open Platinum Rate Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗
Wedding rings and engagement settings often use .950 platinum. Calculate melt to evaluate buyer offers.
Recyclers pay for the platinum / palladium / rhodium content. Weight × purity × spot gives a rough metal value for negotiation.
Platinum bars (.9995 / .9999) trade at small premiums to spot. Weight × spot gives the floor price.
Distinguishing platinum from white gold matters — they look similar but values differ. Stamp + density check + this calculator clarifies.

Enter spot platinum price — Per gram or per troy ounce. Platinum has often traded below gold since ~2015 — verify the current rate. Pick weight unit — Grams, ounces, kilograms. Enter purity — .950 (standard jewelry), .900 (some hallmarks), .850 (lower jewelry standard), .9995 (investment bars). Compute melt value — weight × purity × spot price. Compare to gold equivalent — Optional: see what equivalent gold would cost for the same weight; useful when pricing custom rings.

Input: 8 g of .950 platinum at $30/g spot Output: 8 × 0.95 × $30 = $228 melt value Input: 1 troy oz .9995 platinum bar at $950/oz Output: 1 × 0.9995 × $950 = $949.53 melt value Input: 15 g of .900 platinum at $30/g Output: 15 × 0.90 × $30 = $405

Why does platinum sometimes trade below gold? Platinum demand is heavily industrial (catalytic converters); when auto demand softens or palladium substitutes, platinum drops. Gold has consistent investment / jewelry demand. How can I tell platinum from white gold? Stamp ("PT", "Plat", "950") plus density. Platinum is significantly denser (21.45 g/cc) than white gold (~14–16 g/cc). XRF or acid testing confirms. Is platinum jewelry hypoallergenic? Generally yes — platinum alloys typically use ruthenium, iridium, or cobalt rather than nickel, avoiding the most common metal allergies. Why is the buyer offering only 50% of spot? Platinum buyers take large margins because the market is illiquid for jewelry. Specialty refiners pay closer to 90% of spot but require minimum lots. Can I refine platinum at home? No — process involves aqua regia and is dangerous. Send to a professional refiner. Does the calculator handle platinum-iridium alloys? Yes — enter the platinum percentage as the purity. Iridium has its own value but is small; calculator rounds in your favour by ignoring it.

Confirm the stamp before trusting purity — "PLAT" alone in the US implies at least .950; international standards vary. Platinum is heavy — check density as a quick authenticity test before shipping for sale. Spot prices for platinum are noisier than gold; lock at the moment of transaction. For catalytic-converter scrap, the small piece often contains more total precious metal than visible — weigh the whole substrate. For investment bars, prefer recognised refiners (PAMP, Valcambi) — third-party bars trade at deeper discounts.

A profit margin calculator is a tool that expresses your profit as a percentage of revenue, computing three standard margins from a simplified income statement: gross margin, operating margin, and net margin. Gross margin is revenue minus cost of goods sold, divided by revenue; operating margin subtracts operating expenses from gross profit before dividing; net margin takes what remains after interest, taxes, and other items. Because each margin is a share of sales rather than an absolute dollar figure, it lets you compare businesses of very different sizes on the same footing. Everything runs in your browser, and every result depends on how you choose to categorize your costs. Try it now Open Profit Margin Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗

A dollar figure alone hides scale — a shop earning $50,000 profit on $1 million in sales is far leaner than one earning the same profit on $200,000. Expressing profit as a percentage of revenue puts both on equal footing, so you can benchmark your business against a competitor, a franchise average, or your own past year regardless of how big each one happens to be.

Splitting profit into gross, operating, and net margins shows exactly where money disappears between the top and bottom line. A healthy gross margin sitting above a thin operating margin points at overhead — rent, salaries, marketing — rather than production costs. Reading the three margins together tells you whether to renegotiate with suppliers, trim operating expenses, or look at interest and tax drag.

Because the calculator updates the instant you change a number, you can model a decision before committing to it. Raise a price and watch gross margin lift; add a hire to operating expenses and see the operating margin compress. It turns a vague hunch about profitability into concrete percentages, making it easier to decide whether a discount, a bulk supplier deal, or a new cost is worth taking on.

Margins vary enormously by sector — a grocer may run a low single-digit net margin while a software firm runs 20% or more, so any number is only meaningful next to industry norms. Use the tool to compute your own margins, then compare them against typical figures for your field rather than an unrelated business, which is the only fair yardstick for whether you are doing well.

When you pitch a bank or an investor, they expect profit stated as margins, not just totals. Running your income statement through the calculator gives you gross, operating, and net percentages to drop into a summary, and it helps you anticipate the questions that a thin operating margin or a shrinking net margin will raise, so you can answer them before anyone else spots the gap.
documents.s: Prepare figures for lenders or investors

documents.t: Enter revenue — Type total sales revenue for the period; every margin is a share of this figure, so it anchors all three results. Enter cost of goods sold (COGS) — Add the direct costs of producing what you sold, such as materials and direct labour; revenue minus this gives gross profit. Enter operating expenses — Include overhead like rent, salaries, and marketing; subtracting these from gross profit gives operating profit. Enter interest, taxes, and other items — Add financing costs, taxes, and any other deductions to arrive at the net profit that reaches the bottom line. Read the three margins — The tool divides each profit level by revenue and shows gross, operating, and net margin as percentages side by side.

Input: Revenue $200,000, COGS $120,000, operating expenses $50,000, interest/taxes $10,000 Output: Gross 40%, Operating 15%, Net 10% Input: Revenue $1,000,000, COGS $700,000, operating expenses $200,000, other $50,000 Output: Gross 30%, Operating 10%, Net 5% Input: Revenue $80,000, COGS $30,000, operating expenses $45,000 Output: Gross 62.5%, Operating 6.25%, Net 6.25%

What is the difference between gross, operating, and net margin? Gross margin subtracts only the direct cost of goods sold; operating margin also subtracts overhead like rent and salaries; net margin subtracts everything else, including interest and taxes. Each is that profit divided by revenue, so they step down from the broadest measure of profitability to the narrowest. What counts as cost of goods sold? COGS is the direct cost of producing what you sold — raw materials, components, and direct labour. Overhead such as rent, office salaries, and marketing belongs in operating expenses instead. Where you draw that line changes your gross margin, so be consistent. Which margin matters most? It depends on the question. Gross margin shows how profitable your core product is before overhead; operating margin reflects how well you run the business day to day; net margin is what finally reaches the owner. Most people watch all three, because a change in one points at a different problem. Is a higher margin always better? Usually, but not always. A very high margin achieved by underpaying staff or skimping on reinvestment can be fragile, and some high-volume, low-margin models are extremely successful. Margins are a health indicator to read in context, not a single score to maximize blindly. Why do my margins differ from a competitor’s? Different cost structures, pricing, scale, and accounting choices all move margins, and a rival may classify costs differently than you do. Compare against businesses in the same industry with similar models, and treat a gap as a question to investigate rather than a verdict. Is this financial advice or an audit? No. This is an educational estimate based on the numbers you enter. It does not check your books, apply accounting standards, or account for depreciation, one-off items, or how you categorize costs. For decisions that matter, work with an accountant. Is my financial data uploaded anywhere? No. Every calculation runs in your browser. Nothing you type is sent to a server or stored.

Use figures from the same period for revenue, COGS, and expenses so the margins line up. Be consistent about what goes in COGS versus operating expenses, or your gross margin will drift. Compare margins within your own industry, not across unrelated sectors. Track the trend across several periods rather than reading a single snapshot. Investigate a widening gap between gross and net margin — it usually signals rising overhead or financing costs.

A property tax calculator is a tool that estimates the annual property tax on a home by multiplying its taxable assessed value by the local tax rate, usually expressed in mills. The assessed value is derived from market value times an assessment ratio, then reduced by any homestead or other exemptions. Because a mill is one-tenth of a percent, a 20-mill rate equals 2 percent of taxable value. Rates, ratios, and exemptions are set locally and vary widely from one county or town to the next, so this tool is a starting estimate rather than a bill. It runs entirely in your browser and is not tax advice — it cannot know your specific jurisdiction’s rate, special assessments, or the outcome of any appeal. Try it now Open Property Tax Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗

When shopping for a house, property tax can add hundreds of dollars to a monthly payment beyond principal and interest. Plugging in a listing’s asking price, a rough assessment ratio, and the area’s millage rate gives an annual estimate you can divide by twelve to fold into your budget. Confirm the real figures with the county before you rely on them, since the true bill depends on local specifics this tool does not have.
documents.s: Budget for a home you’re considering

documents.t: When your county mails a new assessed value, it helps to see what the tax would be at the published millage rate. If the estimate jumps sharply from last year, that is a cue to review the assessment for errors and weigh whether an appeal is worthwhile. The tool only shows the arithmetic — whether an appeal succeeds, and any resulting change, is entirely up to your local assessor’s process.

Two homes at the same price can carry very different tax bills because millage rates and assessment ratios differ by jurisdiction. Running each town’s numbers side by side turns a vague sense that "taxes are higher over there" into a concrete annual difference, helping you weigh location trade-offs. The calculator does not know either town’s exact rate, ratio, or exemptions, so you supply those values yourself.

Many states reduce the taxable value of an owner-occupied primary residence through a homestead exemption. Entering the exemption amount shows how much it trims the annual bill, making it clear why registering for exemptions you qualify for is worth the paperwork. Eligibility rules and dollar amounts are set locally, so treat the reduction shown here as illustrative until you confirm what your jurisdiction actually grants.
documents.s: See the effect of a homestead exemption

documents.t: Lenders often collect property tax monthly into an escrow account, so the annual estimate divided by twelve approximates that slice of your payment. Seeing the figure ahead of time helps you anticipate the full monthly cost and avoid surprise at closing. The lender’s own escrow analysis, based on the real tax bill and any cushion they require, is what ultimately governs the amount collected.
documents.s: Estimate the escrow portion of a payment

documents.t: Enter the market value — Type the home’s estimated market or appraised value — the county’s starting point before any ratio or exemption is applied. Set the assessment ratio — Enter the ratio your jurisdiction uses (for example 80% or 100%); assessed value equals market value times this ratio. Subtract exemptions — Add any homestead or other exemption amount that reduces the assessed value before tax is figured. Enter the millage rate — Provide the local rate in mills; remember one mill is one-tenth of a percent, so 20 mills is 2 percent. Read the estimated tax — The tool multiplies taxable assessed value by the rate and shows the estimated annual property tax and effective percentage.

Input: Market value $300,000, ratio 100%, no exemption, 20 mills Output: Estimated tax $6,000/yr Input: Market value $300,000, ratio 80%, $25,000 homestead, 25 mills Output: Estimated tax $5,375/yr Input: Market value $450,000, ratio 100%, no exemption, 12 mills Output: Estimated tax $5,400/yr

What is a mill or millage rate? A mill is one-tenth of one percent, or $1 of tax per $1,000 of taxable value. So a 20-mill rate is 2 percent. Local governments set the millage rate to fund schools, roads, and services, and it can change each year. What is the difference between market value and assessed value? Market value is roughly what the home would sell for. Assessed value is what the taxing authority uses, calculated as market value times an assessment ratio and then reduced by exemptions. Property tax is figured on the taxable assessed value, not the market value. Why is my real bill different from this estimate? Because rates, assessment ratios, and exemptions are set locally and this tool uses the values you type. It also cannot include special assessments, voter-approved levies, or district-specific charges. Always confirm with your county assessor or tax office. Is property tax tied to a federal tax year? No. Property tax is a local levy assessed and billed on each jurisdiction’s own schedule, unrelated to the federal income-tax year. This estimate simply annualizes the amount at the rate you provide. Does it tell me if I can appeal my assessment? No. It only estimates the tax from the numbers you enter. Whether to appeal, how, and what the result would be are governed by your local assessor’s appeal process, which varies by jurisdiction. How do I find my millage rate and assessment ratio? They are published by your county or municipal tax office, often on your assessment notice, your latest tax bill, or the assessor’s website. Use those official figures rather than a guess for a meaningful estimate. Is anything I enter uploaded? No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser; nothing you type is sent to a server or stored.

Use your official assessment notice for the market value, ratio, and exemptions rather than estimates. Convert a percentage rate to mills by multiplying by 10 — 1.5% is 15 mills. Check every exemption you may qualify for (homestead, senior, veteran, disability); they can meaningfully lower the bill. Add any known special assessments separately — this estimate covers only the general millage. Confirm the final figure with your county tax office before budgeting or appealing.

A quarterly estimated tax calculator is a tool that estimates the four federal estimated tax payments you may owe in 2025 using the IRS Form 1040-ES safe-harbor rule. To avoid an underpayment penalty, the safe harbor lets you pay the smaller of 90% of this year’s total tax or 100% of last year’s tax — 110% if last year’s adjusted gross income (AGI) was over $150,000 ($75,000 if married filing separately). This tool subtracts your expected withholding and divides the remainder into four instalments. If you expect to owe under $1,000 after withholding, no estimated payments are required. It runs in your browser as a 2025 estimate, not tax advice. Try it now Open Quarterly Estimated Tax Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗

The IRS can charge a penalty if you pay too little through the year, even when you settle the balance by April. Meeting a safe harbor — 90% of the current year, or 100%/110% of the prior year — protects you from that penalty. This tool shows the smaller safe-harbor target so you can pay enough across the four quarters to stay clear of it.

When income arrives without withholding — freelancing, dividends, rental, or capital gains — you are expected to pre-pay tax in quarterly instalments. Entering your prior-year tax and expected withholding turns that obligation into four concrete numbers and dates, so you can budget for each payment instead of being surprised by a large bill and penalty at filing time.
documents.s: Budget for freelance or investment income

documents.t: If your income is hard to predict, the prior-year safe harbor is often easier: pay 100% of last year’s total tax (110% for higher earners) regardless of how this year turns out. Entering last year’s figure lets the tool base your instalments on a known number, which many people find simpler than forecasting the current year from scratch.
documents.s: Use last year’s tax when this year is uncertain

documents.t: Not everyone must make estimated payments. If you expect to owe less than $1,000 after subtracting withholding, none are required. By entering your expected tax and withholding, the tool tells you whether you cross that $1,000 threshold, so you do not schedule quarterly payments you do not actually need to make.
documents.s: Check whether you even need to pay

documents.t: Estimated tax is not one annual payment but four, on a schedule that is not evenly spaced. The 2025 federal due dates are April 15, June 16, and September 15 of 2025 and January 15 of 2026. Seeing each date next to its amount makes it easy to set calendar reminders and pay each instalment on time.

Enter this year’s expected total tax — Provide your estimated 2025 total federal tax; the tool takes 90% of it as one safe-harbor option. It does not compute this figure for you. Enter last year’s total tax — Add your 2024 total tax, which the tool uses at 100% — or 110% if your prior-year AGI was over the threshold — as the other safe-harbor option. Flag your prior-year income level — Indicate whether last year’s AGI exceeded $150,000 ($75,000 if married filing separately) so the correct 100% or 110% factor is used. Subtract expected withholding — Enter tax you expect to be withheld from paycheques, pensions, or other sources; the tool removes it before splitting the balance. Read the four quarterly amounts — It picks the smaller safe-harbor target, subtracts withholding, divides by four, and lists each amount beside its 2025 due date.

Input: This year $12,000; last year $10,000; AGI under $150k; $4,000 withheld Output: Safe harbor $10,000 − $4,000 = $6,000 → about $1,500 per quarter Input: Last year $30,000; AGI over $150k; $10,000 withheld Output: 110% × $30,000 = $33,000 − $10,000 = $23,000 → about $5,750 per quarter Input: Expected tax $3,500; withholding $2,800 Output: Owe about $700 after withholding — no estimated payments required

What is the safe-harbor rule? It is the IRS threshold that avoids an underpayment penalty: pay the smaller of 90% of this year’s total tax or 100% of last year’s tax through withholding and estimated payments. If last year’s AGI was over $150,000 ($75,000 if married filing separately), the prior-year figure becomes 110%. When are 2025 estimated taxes due? The four federal due dates are April 15, 2025; June 16, 2025; September 15, 2025; and January 15, 2026. When the 15th falls on a weekend or holiday the deadline shifts to the next business day, which is why June 16 replaces June 15 in 2025. Do I have to make estimated payments? Not always. If you expect to owe less than $1,000 after subtracting withholding, no estimated payments are required. People whose withholding already covers a safe harbor also may not need to pay anything extra. Does this calculate my total tax for me? No. You enter your expected total tax (and last year’s tax); the tool does not figure your income tax itself. Estimate those separately or take them from your prior return before using this calculator. Does it cover state estimated taxes? No. This tool is federal only and ignores state estimated taxes, which have their own rules, amounts, and due dates. Check your state’s tax agency if you also owe state estimated payments. What if my income changes during the year? You can re-run the estimate whenever your income shifts and adjust the remaining payments. The IRS also allows an annualized-income method for uneven income, which this simple tool does not perform. Is this tax advice? No. It is a 2025 (TY2025) educational estimate of federal estimated payments using the standard safe-harbor rule. Your situation may differ; consult a tax professional or the IRS Form 1040-ES instructions for your actual obligation.

Use the prior-year safe harbor when your income is hard to predict — it relies on a known number. Count withholding from a job or pension: it reduces, and can even eliminate, what you owe each quarter. Note that the payment schedule is uneven — the periods are not all exactly three months apart. Re-run the estimate mid-year if your income jumps, and top up the remaining instalments. Add your state estimated taxes separately; this tool covers federal payments only.

A retirement calculator is a tool that projects how large a retirement nest egg your current savings could grow into, then estimates the yearly income that pot might support. It takes your current savings, your monthly contributions, an assumed annual investment return, and the years until you retire, and compounds them forward to a projected balance. It then applies the 4% "safe withdrawal" guideline to estimate a sustainable annual income, and discounts the result for inflation so you see both a nominal (future-dollar) figure and a real (today’s-dollar) figure. Long-horizon projections swing widely with the return and inflation you assume, so treat every number as an illustration, not a promise. This is not financial advice. Try it now Open Retirement Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗

"Save for retirement" is hard to act on; a projected balance and the income it could produce make it concrete. Seeing that a given monthly contribution grows to a specific nest egg — and roughly what yearly income the 4% rule draws from it — helps you judge whether your current pace is on track or needs adjusting well before retirement arrives.
documents.s: Turn a vague goal into a target number

documents.t: Because the projection updates from your inputs, you can try different monthly contributions and watch how much difference an extra amount makes over decades. Compounding rewards consistency and time, so a modest increase sustained for many years often moves the final balance far more than people expect, which is a powerful reason to start early.
documents.s: Compare contribution levels side by side

documents.t: A seven-figure future balance can be misleading because inflation erodes what money buys. The real, inflation-adjusted figure translates the projection into today’s dollars, giving a more honest sense of the lifestyle it could fund. Comparing the nominal and real numbers side by side shows just how much inflation quietly matters over a long horizon.
documents.s: See today’s-dollar value, not just a big number

documents.t: Because long projections are so sensitive to the rates you choose, entering a more cautious return and a higher inflation rate reveals how fragile an optimistic plan can be. Running both an optimistic and a conservative scenario brackets a realistic range of outcomes, which is far more useful for planning than trusting a single confident-looking number.
documents.s: Stress-test your return and inflation assumptions

documents.t: The 4% rule is a rough guideline that a portfolio might sustain annual withdrawals of about 4% of its starting value. Seeing that figure attached to your projected balance helps you gauge whether the income would cover your expected needs, while reminding you that the rule is a starting assumption, not a guarantee that the money will last.

Enter your current savings — Start with the total you have already set aside for retirement across your accounts. Add your monthly contribution — Enter how much you plan to add each month; this is compounded along with your starting balance. Set your assumed annual return — Choose a realistic growth rate for your investments — this single input has an outsized effect on the result. Enter years to retirement and inflation — Give the number of years until you retire and an expected inflation rate so the tool can show today’s-dollar values. Read the projected balance and income — The calculator shows the nominal and inflation-adjusted nest egg and applies the 4% rule to estimate a sustainable annual income.

Input: $50,000 saved, $500/mo, 7% return, 30 years, 3% inflation Output: ≈ $990,000 nominal (~$408,000 in today’s dollars) Input: $0 saved, $300/mo, 6% return, 40 years, 2.5% inflation Output: ≈ $598,000 nominal (~$223,000 in today’s dollars) Input: Same inputs but a 5% return instead of 7% Output: The projected balance drops sharply

What is the 4% rule? It is a rule of thumb from retirement research suggesting that withdrawing about 4% of your portfolio’s starting value each year, then adjusting for inflation, has historically had a reasonable chance of lasting roughly 30 years. It is a guideline based on past markets, not a guarantee for the future. Why does the tool show nominal and real numbers? The nominal figure is the raw future balance; the real figure discounts it for inflation to show what it would be worth in today’s dollars. Over decades, inflation makes a big number buy much less, so the real value is usually the more meaningful one for planning. How accurate is a 30- or 40-year projection? It is an illustration, not a forecast. Real returns vary year to year, inflation shifts, and contributions change. The result depends heavily on assumptions you cannot know in advance, so use it to compare scenarios rather than to predict an exact balance. What return rate should I use? There is no correct number. Long-run stock returns have often been cited around 7% before inflation, but the future may differ and your mix of investments matters. Because the result is so sensitive to this input, it is wise to run a conservative rate as well. Does it account for taxes and fees? No. This is a simplified projection that ignores taxes, investment fees, employer matches, and Social Security or pensions. A real plan should factor those in, which is where a financial professional can help. Is my data saved or shared? No. All calculations happen in your browser. Nothing you enter is uploaded or stored by the tool. Is this financial advice? No. It is an educational estimate. For decisions about how much to save, how to invest, or when to retire, consult a qualified financial advisor who can consider your full circumstances.

Run at least two scenarios — one optimistic, one conservative — to bracket a realistic range. Focus on the today’s-dollar (real) figure; the big nominal number overstates your future buying power. Small increases to your monthly contribution compound heavily over decades — try nudging it up. Remember the projection ignores taxes, fees, and other income such as Social Security or a pension. Revisit the calculation yearly and update it as your savings, contributions, and goals change.

A return-on-investment (ROI) calculator measures the profit of an investment as a percentage of the cost — the simple formula (net gain / cost) × 100% — and (more usefully for multi-year holdings) the annualised return / CAGR (compound annual growth rate) (end value / start value)^(1/years) − 1, which lets you compare investments held for different periods on equal footing. The ZTools ROI Calculator runs entirely in the browser, supports both simple and CAGR modes, accepts intermediate cash flows for IRR-style scenarios (approximation), and is the right starting point for evaluating real-estate flips, stock holdings, business ventures, and side projects. Try it now Open ROI Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗

Stock A: bought $5K, sold $7K after 3 years. Stock B: bought $5K, sold $6K after 1 year. Simple ROI says A wins (40% vs 20%); CAGR says B wins (20% vs 11.9%). The right metric depends on the question.
Bought house for $200K + $30K rehab; sold for $280K. ROI = ($280K − $230K) / $230K = 21.7%. Annualise by holding period for fair comparison to other investments.
Initial cost $10K, gross profit over 18 months $14K. ROI = 40% simple; CAGR ≈ 25% annualised.
Spent $5K on ads, attributed $20K in net revenue. Marketing ROI = 300%. Useful for budget allocation.

Enter investment cost — Initial cash outlay. Include all costs (purchase price + fees + improvements). Enter end value — Sale price net of selling costs, OR current value if still holding. Enter holding period — For annualised return / CAGR. Skip for simple ROI. Compute — Simple ROI: (end − cost) / cost. CAGR: (end / cost)^(1/years) − 1. Both shown. Interpret — Compare to benchmarks: stock-market average ~10%, savings ~4%. Your ROI vs alternative use of capital is the real comparison.

Input: Cost $10K, end value $15K, 3 years Output: Simple ROI 50% · CAGR ≈ 14.5% per year Input: Cost $50K (including $5K fees), sold $80K, 5 years Output: Simple ROI 60% · CAGR ≈ 9.86% Input: Marketing campaign: spent $5K, generated $20K profit Output: ROI 300%

When should I use simple ROI vs CAGR? Simple ROI for "did this make money overall?". CAGR for comparing to other investments — annualises the return so a 1-year and 10-year holding can be fairly compared. Should I include opportunity cost? For sophisticated analysis, yes. The proper comparison is "ROI vs ROI of next-best alternative use of capital". Simple ROI alone can flatter losing investments. How do I handle dividends or rental income? Add total cash distributions to the gain. So end value + dividends − cost = net gain. The calculator supports this via the cash-flow input. Does it handle inflation? Returns nominal ROI. To get real ROI, subtract expected inflation (e.g., 3%) from CAGR. What is a "good" ROI? Depends on risk. Low-risk savings ~4–5% beats inflation. Stock market average ~10% nominal. High-risk angel investments may target 30%+ — but lose 50% of the time. Can it compute IRR? Approximately for equal-period cash flows. True IRR (irregular cash flows over time) needs a more advanced tool.

Always include all costs (fees, taxes, improvements) — partial cost inputs flatter the ROI. For multi-year holdings, prefer CAGR over simple ROI for fair comparison. Compare to a benchmark (S&P 500 over the same period) — beating it consistently is harder than it looks. Account for risk — a 20% return on volatile crypto and a 20% return on a savings account are not comparable. For business investments, factor in your time as a cost — many "high ROI" side projects pay below minimum wage when time is included.

A sales tax calculator is a tool that works out the tax on a purchase by multiplying the amount by the combined sales tax rate — the state base rate plus any local city, county, or district taxes. It also runs in reverse: given a tax-inclusive total, it divides by one plus the rate to recover the original pre-tax price and the tax portion. This calculator starts from approximate statewide base rates as a convenience, but localities add their own tax, so your real combined rate may be higher. Five states — Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon — levy no statewide sales tax. It is an estimate rather than tax advice, it does not track product-specific exemptions or exact local district rates, and it runs in your browser. Try it now Open Sales Tax Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗

Shelf and online prices in the US usually exclude sales tax, so the amount at checkout is higher than the sticker. Entering the price and your combined rate shows the tax and the final total, which is handy for staying on budget or checking a receipt. Because local rates vary by address, confirm your exact combined rate for where the sale actually takes place before treating the total as final.
documents.s: Add tax to a price before you buy

documents.t: Sometimes you have a total that already includes tax — a cash receipt or an all-in quote — and need the pre-tax price for an expense report or bookkeeping. Reverse mode divides the total by one plus the rate to split it into the base amount and the tax. This is the correct method; simply subtracting the rate from the total overstates the tax and understates the base price.

Because statewide base rates range from zero to over 7 percent, the same purchase costs noticeably more in one state than another. Running the numbers helps with decisions like where to make a large purchase or how to compare quotes. The tool uses statewide base rates only, though, so it cannot capture the local add-ons that often make the real difference between two nearby areas.
documents.s: Compare the tax bite across states

documents.t: Freelancers and small businesses that add sales tax to an invoice can compute the line quickly by entering the subtotal and rate. The result is an estimate to help you draft the document. Your actual obligation depends on your registered rate, where you have nexus, and whether the specific product or service is taxable — none of which this general calculator determines.
documents.s: Estimate tax for invoices and quotes

documents.t: The add and reverse modes make a clear teaching example for how a percentage is applied and then undone. Students can see why recovering a pre-tax price is a division by one plus the rate, not a subtraction, and can experiment with different rates to build intuition. It is a learning aid for the arithmetic, not a tool for actual tax filing or compliance.
documents.s: Teach how percentages and tax work

documents.t: Choose add or reverse mode — Add tax to a pre-tax price, or reverse a total that already includes tax to recover the original price. Enter the amount — Type the pre-tax price in add mode, or the tax-inclusive total in reverse mode. Set your combined rate — Start from the statewide base rate the tool suggests, then adjust it to your true combined state-plus-local rate. Read the tax and total — Add mode shows the tax and final total; reverse mode shows the tax and the recovered pre-tax price. Verify locally if it matters — For a real purchase or filing, confirm the exact combined rate for the transaction’s address, since local taxes are not built in.

Input: $100.00, combined rate 8.25% (add mode) Output: Tax $8.25 — total $108.25 Input: $108.25 total, rate 8.25% (reverse mode) Output: Pre-tax $100.00 — tax $8.25 Input: $59.99 in Oregon (no statewide sales tax) Output: Tax $0.00 — total $59.99

How is sales tax calculated? Multiply the pre-tax amount by the combined sales tax rate — the state base rate plus any local taxes. For a $50 item at 7 percent, the tax is $3.50 and the total is $53.50. How does reverse (tax-inclusive) mode work? It divides the tax-inclusive total by one plus the rate. For a $53.50 total at 7 percent, $53.50 ÷ 1.07 = $50.00 pre-tax, leaving $3.50 of tax. Subtracting 7 percent of $53.50 would overstate the tax. Are the built-in rates exact? No. The tool uses approximate statewide base rates as a starting point. Cities, counties, and special districts add their own sales tax, so your actual combined rate is often higher. Always confirm the local rate for the address. Which states have no sales tax? Five states levy no statewide sales tax: Alaska, Delaware, Montana, New Hampshire, and Oregon. Note that some localities in Alaska still impose their own local sales tax. Does it handle exempt items like groceries or clothing? No. Many states tax groceries, clothing, or other categories differently, or exempt them entirely. This tool applies one flat rate and does not model product-specific exemptions or reduced rates. Can I use it for another country’s VAT or GST? The arithmetic is the same — apply a rate, or reverse a tax-inclusive total — so you can enter any rate you like. The built-in base rates and the list of no-tax states are US-specific, however. Is my data uploaded? No. The calculation runs entirely in your browser and nothing is sent to a server or saved.

Look up your exact combined rate by street address, since two nearby addresses can differ. Use reverse mode for receipts that show only a total, without a separate tax line. Remember to divide, not subtract, when removing tax from a tax-inclusive total. Check whether the item is taxable in your state — some categories are exempt or taxed at a special rate. For business filing, rely on your registered rate and a tax professional, not a general estimate.

A savings goal calculator works out the monthly contribution required to reach a target amount by a given deadline — combining any starting balance, monthly contribution, and an expected interest rate (for high-yield savings or low-risk investments) using the future-value-of-annuity formula. The ZTools Savings Goal Calculator runs in the browser, supports both "how much per month?" and "how long will it take?" modes, factors compound interest for realistic high-yield savings projections, and is the right starting point for emergency funds, down-payments, vacations, and any time-bound saving goal. Try it now Open Savings Goal Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗
Target $40,000 in 4 years, $5K already saved, 4% high-yield savings. Calculator returns the required monthly contribution.
Target 6 months of expenses ($24K), 0% in checking, no starting balance, 18-month deadline. $1,333/month required.
A $5K trip in 10 months — $500/month covers it. Quick reality check.
Affordable monthly $300, target $20K — calculator shows it will take ~5 years at low interest, helping reset expectations or boost contributions.

Enter target amount and deadline — How much you want to save and by when. Enter starting balance — Optional — money already saved toward the goal. Enter expected annual rate — 0% for plain savings; 4–5% for high-yield savings; 8% for low-risk index funds (with risk acknowledgement). Compute monthly contribution — Solves the future-value-of-annuity equation for the required monthly amount. Show alternative scenarios — See what happens if you start later, contribute less, or extend the deadline.

Input: Target $40,000 in 48 months, start $5,000, 4% APR Output: Required ~$680/month Input: Target $24,000 in 18 months, start $0, 0% interest Output: Required $1,333/month Input: Target $100,000 in 10 years, start $5,000, 8% expected return Output: Required ~$510/month

Should I use a savings account or invest? For < 3-year horizons, plain savings (low risk). For 5+ years, low-risk investments may beat inflation. Match risk to time horizon — short goals should not lose principal. How do I find a high-yield savings account? Compare published APY across banks. Online banks typically offer 1–2% above brick-and-mortar. APYs change with central-bank rates. Does the calculator account for inflation? No — outputs are nominal. For long-term goals, set the target slightly higher to compensate for purchasing-power loss. What if I cannot afford the required monthly contribution? Either extend the deadline, lower the target, or find more income. The calculator helps you see the tradeoffs explicitly. Can I model irregular contributions? Default is fixed monthly. For lump-sum windfalls, treat them as starting balance increases at the time they arrive. Is the interest rate before or after tax? After-tax APY is what hits your account. Use after-tax rates for honest projections, especially in taxable accounts.

Automate the monthly contribution — automatic transfers ensure the math actually plays out. For short-term goals, prioritise capital preservation; for long-term, accept some volatility for higher returns. Revisit the calculator quarterly — adjust as income or expenses change. Factor inflation for goals 5+ years out — $100K today may not buy what $100K bought a decade ago. Build the emergency fund first, then layer goal-specific savings on top.

A self-employment tax calculator is a tool that estimates the Social Security and Medicare tax you owe on freelance, contractor, or other 1099 net profit for the 2025 tax year. Self-employment (SE) tax is charged at 15.3% on 92.35% of your net profit: 12.4% for Social Security up to the 2025 wage base of $176,100, plus 2.9% for Medicare with no ceiling. Higher earners add a 0.9% Additional Medicare Tax above $200,000 (single), $250,000 (married filing jointly), or $125,000 (married filing separately). Half of the base SE tax is deductible against your income tax. It runs entirely in your browser and is an estimate, not tax advice. Try it now Open Self-Employment Tax Calculator in ZTools. Open ZTools ↗

Employees split Social Security and Medicare with their employer, but as a self-employed person you pay both halves yourself, which is why the SE rate feels high. Entering your expected net profit shows the SE tax alone, separate from income tax, so you can see the true payroll-tax cost of freelancing and set aside a realistic amount before the money is spent.
documents.s: Estimate what a 1099 year really costs

documents.t: Because no employer withholds tax from a contractor cheque, it is easy to under-save and face a large bill at filing time. Multiplying a rough SE rate against each invoice as it arrives helps you park the right share in a separate account. Use this estimate to pick a percentage of every payment to hold back for the Social Security and Medicare portion.
documents.s: Set money aside from each payment

documents.t: If you also draw a regular paycheck, the Social Security wages already taxed there use up part of the $176,100 base, so less of your freelance profit is subject to the 12.4% Social Security piece — though the 2.9% Medicare part still applies to all of it. Entering your W-2 Social Security wages lets the estimate reduce the remaining wage base accordingly.
documents.s: Account for a W-2 job alongside freelancing

documents.t: Half of your base SE tax can be subtracted from income before income tax is figured, softening the overall bite. Seeing that deduction spelled out helps you understand why the headline 15.3% is not the whole story, and reminds you to claim it when you file so you do not overpay your income tax on the same earnings.
documents.s: See the value of the half-SE deduction

documents.t: When weighing a freelance contract against employment, the SE tax changes the real take-home comparison. Running your expected net profit through the calculator shows the Social Security and Medicare cost you would carry alone, so you can compare a contract rate against a salaried job on a more honest, after-payroll-tax basis rather than headline pay.
documents.s: Compare a contract to a salaried role

documents.t: Enter your net profit — Type your expected 2025 self-employment net profit — gross income minus deductible business expenses — which is the figure SE tax is based on. Choose your filing status — Select single, married filing jointly, or married filing separately so the correct Additional Medicare threshold is applied. Add any W-2 Social Security wages — If you also have a job, enter its Social Security wages so the tool subtracts them from the $176,100 base before charging the 12.4% part. Let it apply the 92.35% factor — The calculator multiplies your net profit by 0.9235, then applies 12.4% Social Security up to the wage base and 2.9% Medicare with no cap. Read your SE tax and deduction — It shows total SE tax, any 0.9% Additional Medicare, and the deductible half you can claim against your income tax.

Input: Net profit $50,000, single, no W-2 job Output: SE tax ≈ $7,065; half-SE deduction ≈ $3,532 Input: Net profit $200,000, single, no W-2 job Output: SE tax ≈ $27,193; half-SE deduction ≈ $13,596 Input: Net profit $60,000 plus $150,000 W-2 Social Security wages Output: Reduced Social Security portion; full Medicare still applies

How is self-employment tax calculated? Your net profit is first multiplied by 92.35% (0.9235). That amount is taxed at 12.4% for Social Security up to the 2025 wage base of $176,100 and at 2.9% for Medicare with no upper limit, for a combined 15.3% on earnings below the base. What is the 92.35% factor for? It reflects the employer-share deduction: because employees do not pay SE tax on their employer’s half, the self-employed reduce net profit by 7.65% before the tax applies, which works out to multiplying by 0.9235. What is the Additional Medicare Tax? An extra 0.9% Medicare tax on earnings above $200,000 (single), $250,000 (married filing jointly), or $125,000 (married filing separately). It applies on top of the regular 2.9% Medicare part for higher earners. Does this include my income tax? No. This tool estimates only Social Security and Medicare (SE) tax. It does not compute federal income tax, state tax, tax credits, or the Qualified Business Income (QBI) deduction — those are separate and can change what you actually owe. How does a regular job affect my SE tax? Social Security wages from a W-2 job count toward the same $176,100 base. If your job already used part or all of it, less of your self-employment profit is subject to the 12.4% Social Security portion, though the 2.9% Medicare portion still applies to all of it. Can I deduct any of the SE tax? Yes. Half of your base SE tax is an above-the-line deduction that lowers your taxable income for income-tax purposes. This estimate shows that deductible half so you can remember to claim it when you file. Is this tax advice? No. It is a 2025 (TY2025) educational estimate for US federal SE tax and can differ from your final return. For decisions about your taxes, consult a qualified tax professional or the IRS instructions for Schedule SE.

Base the estimate on net profit — gross income minus business expenses — not your gross revenue. Set aside a share of each payment as it arrives, since no employer withholds SE tax for you. Remember to claim the half-SE deduction at filing so you do not overpay your income tax. Enter W-2 Social Security wages if you also have a job, or the Social Security part may be overstated. Pair this with a separate income-tax and QBI estimate — SE tax is only one piece of what you owe.
